title: My Metrics Update QRC4.2026: Monitor What Matters
author: arnoklein
text:
My Metrics is your personal KPI cockpit inside SAP Analytics Cloud . It is built for users who want to stay on top of their most important numbers without navigating through reports. With the latest updates, we've made it easier to create, configure, and monitor metrics. Here's what's new. 
 Create Metrics Directly from a Model 
 Until now, metrics could only be added from an existing story widget, which meant you first had to build or navigate to a report before you could monitor a KPI. That's no longer the case. You can now create a metric directly from a model within the My Metrics module, giving you more flexibility to define what you want to track from the start. 
 A Redesigned Wizard 
 The new step-by-step wizard walks you through the entire configuration, from selecting your measure and filters to adding variances and thresholds in a structured, intuitive flow. 

 Quick Time Filters 
 Choosing the right time period for a metric was one of the most common friction points. Quick Time Filters improve this with a curated set of ready-to-use options: Current Month, Quarter to Date, Last Quarter, and more, available directly in the filter step. No more static date configuration for the most common use cases. 

 You can also extend the time window for the detailed visualization independently from the base metric to show a broader range on the detailed visualization via time shift. 
 Improved Variable Support 
 Metric creators can now modify variables (e.g. from SAP BW), so that metrics reflect the current variable state, ensuring your KPIs always show the data that's relevant today, not from the moment you set them up. 

 WalkMe Integration 
 New to My Metrics or exploring a feature for the first time? WalkMe integration brings contextual, step-by-step guidance directly into the product. Instead of searching documentation, you get the right help at the right moment, directly inside the UI. 
 Threshold Configuration 
 Monitoring a number is useful. Knowing when it's off track is better. The new threshold configuration lets you define a threshold directly on your metric. Color-coded status indicators make the situation visible at a glance, without having to interpret the raw number every time. And when a threshold is breached, My Metrics notifies you. You can subscribe to and receive threshold-based notifications directly via eMail, Teams or within SAP Analytics Cloud, so you're informed when a KPI moves outside its defined range. 
 Please also take a look at my colleague Jie Deng's blog post about AI-Assisted Metrics Trend Analysis in SAP Analytics Cloud .

title: Ariba Invoicing / CIM: 2-Factor Authentication (Entra-ID) Identity Federation Fix
author: yanina_geist40ced8
text:
1. Problem Description 
 After switching the CIM application in SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS) to use Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) as the identity provider, users reported error messages when trying to access the Ariba Invoicing module. Authentication via the Microsoft login page succeeded, but the application subsequently failed with errors. Error Scenario 
 User authenticates successfully via Microsoft Entra ID (including 2-Factor Authentication / MFA), but receives an error upon reaching the CIM Accounting module. The session cannot be established correctly for the application. 
 2. Root Cause 
 When an external Identity Provider (IdP) such as Microsoft Entra ID is configured in SAP Cloud Identity Services, the Identity Federation settings determine how SAP IAS (Identity Authentication Service) handles the authenticated user session. 
 By default, the Identity Federation configuration is inherited from the parent application. In this case, the inherited settings did not include “Use Identity Authentication user store” — meaning SAP IAS passed the Entra ID token to CIM without resolving the user against its own user store. As a result, CIM could not find a matching user record and returned an error in the Accounting module. 
 3. Authentication Flow (Before & After Fix) 
 Before the fix (broken flow) User → Microsoft Entra ID 
 MFA / 2FA → SAP IAS (CIS) 
 no user store lookup → CIM Accounting 
 ✗ Error IAS receives federated token but cannot map user → session fails in CIM 
 After the fix (working flow) User → Microsoft Entra ID 
 MFA / 2FA → SAP IAS (CIS) 
 user store lookup ✓ → CIM Accounting 
 ✓ Success IAS resolves identity via user store → enriched user context propagated to CIM 
 4. Solution: Step-by-Step Configuration 
 Log into SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS) as an administrator and follow the navigation path below: CIS Admin Console → Applications → CIM → Conditional Authentication → Identity Federation 1 Open the CIS Admin Console 
 Navigate to your SAP Cloud Identity Services admin console (e.g., https://<tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/admin ) and sign in with administrator credentials. 2 Navigate to Applications 
 In the left-hand menu, click Applications & Resources → Applications . 3 Select the CIM Application 
 Search for or scroll to the CIM application in the list and click on it to open its settings. 4 Open Conditional Authentication 
 Within the CIM application settings, select the Conditional Authentication tab. 5 Open Identity Federation 
 Click on Identity Federation within the Conditional Authentication section. 6 Set Configuration Source to “Custom” 
 Under Configuration Source , change from the inherited value to Custom . This overrides the parent application settings for CIM specifically. 7 Enable “Use Identity Authentication user store” 
 Check the Use Identity Authentication user store checkbox. This is the critical fix. Leave Allow Identity Authentication users only and Apply Application Configurations unchecked. 8 Save and test 
 Save the configuration and ask the affected user to log in again via Microsoft Entra ID to confirm the fix. 
 Fig. 1 — Identity Federation settings in SAP CIS for the CIM application (after fix): Configuration Source set to Custom , Use Identity Authentication user store enabled. 
 5. Why This Is the Correct Solution 
 SAP Cloud Identity Services supports Identity Federation : an external IdP (such as Microsoft Entra ID) handles the primary authentication including MFA/2FA, while SAP IAS acts as a broker connecting the authenticated identity to SAP application user records. 
 The setting “Use Identity Authentication user store” controls whether SAP IAS performs a user lookup in its own user store after receiving the federated assertion from Entra ID: Setting Behavior Result 
 Disabled (inherited / unchecked) SAP IAS forwards the Entra ID token to CIM without user store resolution. CIM receives only raw Entra ID attributes. CIM cannot find a matching user → Error 
 Enabled (checked — after fix) SAP IAS looks up the user in its own store (matching by email). The full IAS user profile (including roles and group memberships) is forwarded to CIM. CIM receives enriched user context → Success Technical Background 
 When Entra ID is configured as a Corporate Identity Provider in SAP IAS, it acts as an upstream IdP. The Identity Federation settings determine how the downstream application (CIM) receives user information. Enabling the IAS user store lookup ensures that attributes stored in IAS (roles, groups, application assignments) are correctly propagated to CIM — which is essential for module-level authorization such as access to the Accounting module. 
 6. Configuration Settings Reference Setting Value (After Fix) Explanation 
 Configuration Source Custom Overrides parent application defaults with settings specific to CIM. Prevents unintended inheritance of restrictive parent configuration. 
 Use Identity Authentication user store ✓ Enabled After Entra ID login, IAS matches the user to an existing IAS record. User profile data and application attributes are forwarded to CIM. 
 Allow Identity Authentication users only ✗ Disabled If enabled, only users with a native IAS account (not federated via Entra ID) would be allowed. Leaving disabled permits Entra ID federated users. 
 Apply Application Configurations ✗ Disabled Leave unchecked unless CIM-specific conditional authentication rules need to be applied on top of the federation settings. 
 7. Resolution Confirmation Issue Resolved 
 After applying the above configuration, the user confirmed successful login via Microsoft Entra ID (including 2-Factor Authentication) and unimpeded access to the CIM Accounting module. (Confirmed November 6, 2026) SAP Cloud Identity Services — CIM Identity Feder

title: Generic SOAP Dispatcher in SAP Integration Suite: A Practical Approach
author: khusal810
text:
Introduction 
 Generic dispatcher patterns are not new in the SAP integration world. 
 If you have worked with IDocs or ABAP Proxies , you have probably seen scenarios where multiple interfaces enter through a common integration layer and are then dispatched to the appropriate integration flow. 
 This made me think: 
 Can we do something similar for SOAP interfaces in SAP Integration Suite? 
 Instead of looking at every SOAP interface as an independent integration entry point, can we create a common SOAP dispatcher, identify the incoming service or operation, and route the request to the appropriate integration flow? 
 That is what I wanted to explore. 
 In this blog, I will walk through an approach for building a Generic SOAP Dispatcher using SAP Integration Suite, Cloud Integration . 
 What Are We Trying to Achieve? 
 Let's assume we have multiple SOAP-based interfaces originating from SAP ECC or SAP S/4HANA. 
 A typical implementation may look like this: 
 SOAP Interface 1 → Integration Flow 1 
 SOAP Interface 2 → Integration Flow 2 
 SOAP Interface 3 → Integration Flow 3 
 The idea is to introduce a common dispatcher layer: 
 SAP ECC / S/4HANA 
 ↓ 
 Generic SOAP Endpoint 
 ↓ 
 Generic SOAP Dispatcher 
 ↓ 
 Identify Incoming Request 
 ↓ 
 Determine Routing Key 
 ↓ 
 Dynamic Routing 
 ↓ 
 Target Integration Flow 
 This raises the most important technical question: 
 How does the dispatcher determine which integration flow should receive the incoming SOAP request? 
 The answer lies in the metadata available with the incoming request. Depending on the SOAP service and configuration, attributes such as SOAPAction , HTTP-related headers, request path, or other message metadata may provide information that can be used to derive a routing key. 
 Before designing the routing logic, therefore, the first step is to understand exactly what information reaches Cloud Integration for the SOAP request. 
 Proposed Technical Design 
 The dispatcher is intentionally kept lightweight. It should not contain the actual business integration logic. 
 Its responsibilities are limited to: 
 Receive the SOAP request. 
 Read the available request metadata. 
 Derive a routing key. 
 Validate the routing key. 
 Route the request to the appropriate target integration flow. 
 Reject unsupported requests in a controlled manner. 
 The overall runtime design is: 
 SOAP Sender 
 ↓ 
 GenericSOAPDispatcher 
 ↓ 
 Read Request Metadata 
 ↓ 
 Determine Routing Key 
 ↓ 
 Router 
 ↓ 
 ProcessDirect 
 ↓ 
 Target Integration Flow 
 Step 1: Create the Generic SOAP Dispatcher 
 Let's start by creating an integration flow called: 
 GenericSOAPDispatcher 
 Add a SOAP Sender Adapter and configure the endpoint that will act as the entry point for the dispatcher. 
 The purpose of this integration flow is not to execute business-specific transformation or receiver logic. It acts as the technical entry and dispatching layer. 
 At this stage, rather than immediately building the routing rules, I first wanted to understand what metadata Cloud Integration receives when the SOAP request arrives. 

 Step 2: Inspect the Incoming Request 
 This is where things become interesting. 
 For a generic dispatcher to work, we need a reliable way of distinguishing one incoming SOAP request from another. 
 During development, we can inspect the headers available to the message when the request reaches the integration flow. 
 A temporary Groovy script can help us understand which headers are available: import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message

def Message processData(Message message) {

 def headers = message.getHeaders()
 def messageLog = messageLogFactory.getMessageLog(message)

 if (messageLog != null) {
 headers.each { key, value ->
 messageLog.setStringProperty(
 key.toString(),
 value?.toString()
 )
 }
 }

 return message
} 
 The intention of this script is purely diagnostic: send a test SOAP request and inspect which request-specific values are available in Cloud Integration. 
 Important: I would not recommend logging every incoming header in a production implementation. HTTP and SOAP headers may contain authentication, authorization, session, or other sensitive information. 
 Once the required routing attributes have been identified, logging should be restricted to the minimum information required for monitoring and troubleshooting. 
 Step 3: Derive a Routing Key 
 The dispatcher now needs to convert the request metadata into something that can be used consistently for routing. 
 One candidate is SOAPAction , where the service configuration provides a meaningful and reliable value. 
 For example, assume we have operations such as: 
 CreateOrder 
 UpdateOrder 
 CancelOrder 
 The incoming metadata could conceptually be mapped to an internal routing key: 
 Incoming Operation Routing Key Target Flow 
 CreateOrder CREATE_ORDER CreateOrder_iFlow 
 UpdateOrder UPDATE_ORDER UpdateOrder_iFlow 
 CancelOrder CANCEL_ORDER CancelOrder_iFlow 
 I prefer deriving an internal routing key instead of tightly coupling the rest of the dispatcher directly to the raw SOAPAction value. 
 This gives us a cleaner separation between request identification and message routing . 
 Conceptually: 
 Incoming SOAP Request 
 ↓ 
 Read SOAP Metadata 
 ↓ 
 Derive Routing Key 
 ↓ 
 CREATE_ORDER / UPDATE_ORDER / CANCEL_ORDER 
 ↓ 
 Router 
 Step 4: Configure the Router 
 Once the routing key is available, a standard Router can be used to determine the target integration flow. 
 For example: 
 CREATE_ORDER → CreateOrder_iFlow 

 UPDATE_ORDER → UpdateOrder_iFlow 

 CANCEL_ORDER → CancelOrder_iFlow 
 A Default Route should always be provided. 
 This handles scenarios where the dispatcher receives a request that it does not recognize. 
 Instead of accidentally routing an unidentified request, the dispatcher can terminate processing with a controlled error such as: 
 Unsupported SOAP operation or routing key. 
 The error-handling path can additionally capture non-sensitive diagnostic information such as: 
 Message ID / correlation identifier 
 Routing key 
 Requested operation 
 Error category 
 Timestamp 
 Step 5: Delegate Processing to the Target Integration Flow 
 A key design principle is to keep the dispatcher lightweight . 
 Business-specific mappings, transformations, validations, receiver calls, and orchestration should remain within the corresponding integration flows. 
 The dispatcher should only determine where the request needs to go . 
 For flows deployed within the same Cloud Integration environment, ProcessDirect can be considered as one approach for communication between the dispatcher and the target integration flows. 
 For example: 
 GenericSOAPDispatcher 
 | 
 +-- CREATE_ORDER → ProcessDirect → CreateOrder_iFlow 
 | 
 +-- UPDATE_ORDER → ProcessDirect → UpdateOrder_iFlow 
 | 
 +-- CANCEL_ORDER → ProcessDirect → CancelOrder_iFlow 
 This separation is important because otherwise the generic dispatcher can slowly turn into a large integration flow containing routing, mapping, transformation, receiver connectivity, and business logic for every interface. 

 Where Does SOAMANAGER Fit? 
 Now comes the other important part of this design. 
 If an ABAP-based SAP ECC or SAP S/4HANA system is acting as the SOAP consumer, the relevant Web Service configuration and logical port in SOAMANAGER has to be configured to communicate with the endpoint exposed through SAP Integration Suite. 
 Conceptually, the end-to-end path becomes: 
 ABAP Application / Consumer Proxy 
 ↓ 
 SOAMANAGER Logical Port 
 ↓ 
 SAP Integration Suite SOAP Endpoint 
 ↓ 
 GenericSOAPDispatcher 
 ↓ 
 Determine Routing Key 
 ↓ 
 ProcessDirect 
 ↓ 
 Business Integration Flow 
 ↓ 
 Target System 
 This is an important area to validate during implementation. 
 A generic endpoint does not automatically mean that every SOAP consumer proxy can simply be pointed at the same URL without considering the underlying service configuration. 
 The following aspects still need to be validated for the individual SOAP services: 
 Service definition 
 Binding 
 SOAP operation 
 SOAPAction behavior 
 Logical port configuration 
 Authentication and certificates 
 Request and response contract 
 Therefore, the dispatcher should be viewed as a routing pattern , not as a way of ignoring the individual SOAP service contracts. 
 Error Handling 
 Centralizing the entry point also gives us an opportunity to consistently handle technical routing errors. 
 Some situations worth considering are: 
 Required routing information is missing. 
 SOAPAction or equivalent metadata cannot be mapped to a routing key. 
 The routing key is not configured. 
 The target integration flow is unavailable. 
 The incoming SOAP message is invalid. 
 Authentication or authorization fails. 
 The downstream integration flow returns an error. 
 One important distinction is that the dispatcher should handle dispatching-related failures , while business-specific error handling should continue to remain with the corresponding business integration flow. 
 This keeps the responsibilities of the dispatcher clear. 
 Design Considerations 
 At this point, it may sound attractive to route every SOAP interface through one dispatcher. 
 I would not recommend doing that by default. 
 The pattern should be adopted where it provides a real operational or architectural benefit. 
 Area Benefit / Consideration 
 Entry Point Provides a common entry and routing layer for suitable SOAP interfaces. 
 Routing Centralizes technical dispatching logic. 
 Monitoring Common routing information can improve operational visibility. 
 Error Handling Unsupported or unidentified requests can be handled consistently. 
 Security Different SOAP services may have different authentication and authorization requirements. 
 Performance The dispatcher introduces an additional processing layer. 
 Availability A central dispatcher becomes a shared dependency for all interfaces routed through it. 
 Governance New routing entries need controlled onboarding and ownership. 
 Maintenance An uncontrolled number of routing rules can make the dispatcher difficult to maintain. 
 Service Contract The common dispatcher does not remove the need to respect individual SOAP service contracts. 
 When Would I Use This Pattern? 
 I would consider this pattern when: 
 There are multiple SOAP interfaces following a similar integration pattern. 
 A reliable request attribute can be used to identify the destination. 
 Centralized routing provides a genuine operational benefit. 
 The target business flows can remain independently maintained. 
 Security requirements are compatible with the common entry-point design. 
 For a small number of unrelated SOAP interfaces, dedicated endpoints may still be simpler and easier to maintain. 
 Conclusion 
 So, coming back to the question that started this experiment: 
 Can we implement a generic dispatcher for SOAP interfaces in SAP Integration Suite, similar to patterns we have seen for IDocs and ABAP Proxies? 
 Yes, we can build such a pattern. 
 The technical flow is relatively straightforward: 
 SOAP Request 
 ↓ 
 Generic SOAP Endpoint 
 ↓ 
 Inspect Request Metadata 
 ↓ 
 Derive Routing Key 
 ↓ 
 Router 
 ↓ 
 ProcessDirect 
 ↓ 
 Target Integration Flow 
 The real design decision is not whether we can build it, but whether the pattern makes sense for the integration landscape. 
 A good generic dispatcher should remain a lightweight technical routing layer. It should not become the place where every interface's business logic is implemented. 
 The other important consideration is identifying a stable and reliable routing attribute . SOAPAction can be one candidate, but the exact mechanism should be validated against the actual SOAP service design and runtime behavior. 
 I started exploring this because generic dispatcher patterns are familiar on the IDoc and Proxy side, and I wanted to see how the same idea could be applied to SOAP interfaces in SAP Integration Suite.

title: Discontinuation of the ABAP Cloud Developer Trial
author: lienards
text:
Many developers used the ABAP Cloud Developer Trial to explore ABAP Cloud, experiment, learn, and build. 
 Starting November 17, the ABAP Cloud Developer Trial will no longer be available for download from Docker Hub, and the corresponding Cloud Appliance Template SAP ABAP Platform 2025 developer edition on SAP HANA will no longer be available for creating appliances. 
 Existing ABAP Cloud Developer Trial instances remain usable until their developer licenses expire, but licenses can no longer be extended. 
 Where to go next? 
 We encourage you to explore the free offerings of SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment . For an overview of the available options, see our Get started with SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment: Trial Account vs. Free Tier Option . 
 As SAP partner you can also use the Test, Demo, and Development offerings available through the SAP Partner Portal . 
 A big thank you to everyone who has downloaded, explored, tested, and learned with the ABAP Cloud Developer Trial. We look forward to seeing you on SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment. 
 FAQ 
 Find here some FAQ: 
 What offering can I use to explore and learn ABAP Cloud? 
 Leverage our free offerings of SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment. 
 Will the ABAP Cloud Developer Trial be offered again in future? 
 No. Leverage our free offerings of SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment . 
 I am a partner and I use ABAP Cloud Developer Trial for demos. What can I use as an alternative? 
 Leverage the offerings of the SAP Partner Portal . 
 I am neither an SAP customer nor a partner. What can I use as an alternative? 
 Leverage our free offerings of SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment . 
 What happens to my existing ABAP Cloud Developer Trial instances? 
 Existing instances can be used until the related developer license expires. 
 What happens to my existing CAL instances? 
 Existing instances can be used until the related developer license expires. 
 Are any other CAL templates affected? 
 No, only the Cloud Appliance Template SAP ABAP Platform 2025 developer edition on SAP HANA is affected. 
 Will it be possible to extend the developer license for existing instances? 
 No.

title: Build, Buy, or Configure? Closing an ERP Gap Without Adding a Vendor - Part 2
author: pascale_mwavaga
text:
Three ways to close a gap, and only one of them fit 
 In Part 1 , I described the gap: SAP Business One cannot print inventory barcode labels from a posted Goods Receipt PO. 
 This post is about what happened next: I did not design the solution immediately and wrote nothing. I spent time deciding which of three roads to take, then living with the consequences of that choice through the solution's design. 

 Approach 
 What it gives you 
 What it costs an SMB (Small and Medium-sized Business) 

 Buy a label management product 
 Proper label designer, printer fleet management, mature ZPL handling 
 New license line, new integration surface, a tool only one person learns 

 Build a custom SDK add-on 
 Exactly the behavior you specify, no third-party limits 
 A developer you do not have, and an add-on that must be re-tested every upgrade 

 Configure what is already owned 
 No new vendor, no new skillset, maintainable by any B1 consultant 
 You inherit the limits of the tools you have 

 For a large enterprise, buying is usually the right choice. Label management is a real discipline, and the products are good at it. 
 For this client, it was the wrong answer, not because of the license cost. It was wrong because of what I call the second-consultant test: when I leave, can the next person who touches this system understand it, change it, and not be afraid of it? 
 A purchased label engine means the next consultant needs to know SAP Business One and that product. A custom add-on means they need a developer. Crystal Reports and B1UP mean they need skills that every SAP Business One consultant already has. 
 That test is a luxury in enterprise work and a survival requirement in the SMB segment. SMBs change consultants. They change partners. They go eighteen months between touching a system. Anything that only one person understands is a liability with a delay fuse on it. 
 So: configure. Use Crystal Reports for the label itself, Boyum B1UP for the user interaction, and the Zebra printer as a plain Windows printer. 
 The architecture, end to end 

 The Universal Function is highlighted because it is the hinge. It is the only component that talks to both the SAP form above it and the report below it, so it is where almost every design decision ended up: what values to ask for, in what order, with what defaults, and what to do when one of them doesn't exist. 
 Four questions, and why each one is a business requirement 
 The popup asks the user four things. Every one of them exists because a real situation on the floor demanded it, and I think the mapping is worth spelling out, because this is where a technical design either absorbs the warehouse's reality or fights it. 

 What the popup asks 
 Why it has to ask 

 Item 
 A GRPO regularly has eight or twelve lines. Some items in the list could have a different item code. 

 Bin location 
 A receipt can be split across bins. The label has to say where this particular stock went, not where the item usually lives. 

 Lot / batch 
 Some materials are batch-managed and some are not, and both arrive on the same truck. 

 Number of copies 

 Three quantities of an item are received into stock, they are of the same lot, and are placed into the same bin. This means one label printed three times. 
 The button sits in the document footer, next to SAP's own OK and Cancel. Every standard button is still present and still in its usual place, which is exactly the point of the next section. 
 The same label in the Crystal Reports designer. Five fields and a barcode on a small canvas: the entire output side of this solution. 
 The whole user interaction: four fields and an OK button. Note the bin location here reads 00WH-00-ZZ-00-1, while the printed label above shows only 00-ZZ-00-1. The warehouse prefix is stripped on the label by a display formula in the report, because the people reading the label already know which warehouse they are standing in and the field is narrow 
 The design decision I would make again 
 For my first version, I put the button on the form using B1UP's Function Button feature. It worked, and then on some machines the GRPO form resized itself, and the standard SAP buttons along the bottom vanished. 
 The fix was to switch to the Item Placement Tool and connect it to the Universal Function through a Validation configuration instead. Slightly more configuration, three objects rather than one, and the standard form layout is untouched. 
 As all consultants know, users have little tolerance for a system that behaves unpredictably. 
 One small thing that matters more than it should 
 The Boyum variables popup ships with a default title: Define Survey Variables. If you leave it, that is what your warehouse team reads every single time they print a label. 
 Set a title. I used Print GRPO Labels. It takes ten seconds and it is the difference between a feature that feels built for them and a feature that feels like a developer tool someone left switched on. 
 Conclusion 
 What this solution does is unremarkable: a button, a dialog, a report, a printer. What shaped it was the time spent choosing among three roads, and a single question: when I leave, can the next person who touches this system maintain it? 
 That question ruled out both obvious answers. A purchased label engine would have been more capable, and would have left the client dependent on a product nobody there knows. A custom add-on would have fitted exactly, and would have left them dependent on a developer they do not employ. Configuring tools they already owned was the least impressive of the three options and the only one that survives my leaving. 
 Four parameters, three configuration objects, one Crystal report, no custom code. For an SMB (Small and Medium-sized Business) running SAP Business One as its entire stack, that is usually the shape a workable answer takes. 
 In Part 3, I will go through the nine things that broke along the way, including one that showed me my data model had quietly assumed every item was batch-managed.

title: Smarter Compliance Management: Introducing Exemptions in Cloud ALM Configuration & Security Analysis
author: RamyaHV
text:
The Reality of Enterprise Compliance 
 In any large SAP landscape, achieving 100% compliance on every security check, on every system, always, is rarely realistic. Software version limitations, ongoing implementation projects, formally accepted risks, and vendor timelines all create situations where a system legitimately cannot meet a requirement within a given timeframe. 
 In many organisations, Security Officers may find themselves facing an uncomfortable trade-off, either living with compliance reports with "false failures" that erode trust in the data or removing systems from check scope entirely and losing visibility. Neither option is acceptable for serious security governance. 
 Exemptions in SAP Cloud ALM Configuration & Security Analysis (CSA) changes that equation. 

 What Are Exemptions? 
 Exemptions are a formal, auditable mechanism that allows Security Officers to override non-compliant check results for specific systems, services, or configuration item values within a defined time window. 
 This enables CSA to produce two independently queryable views of your landscape: 
 Security Report -> The actual security posture - raw check results, no overrides 
 Compliance Report-> Process compliance - reflecting formally accepted deviations and grace periods 
 Both views coexist. You never lose sight of the real security state, while compliance reporting stays clean and meaningful. 

 When Do You Need an Exemption? 
 Some example real-world scenarios drive this feature: 
 Grace Period for a Newly Introduced Requirement : A new security note arrives, and IT teams need time to roll it out across dozens of systems. A centrally defined grace period applies, reporting systems as compliant during the transition window rather than immediately flagging everything as non-compliant. 
 Formally Accepted Risk: Some systems simply cannot satisfy a requirement due to a software version constraint, a third-party dependency, or implementation effort that outweighs the risk. After formal risk acceptance, Security Officers can overrule the check status for those specific systems with a time boundary that enforces the organization's periodic review cadence. 
 Acceptable Deviations During Validation : During a validation review, certain configuration items deviate from the compliance rule but are deemed acceptable. For example, specific user IDs with special authorizations or known destinations used for a defined purpose. Security Officers can allow-list those specific values to keep compliance reports grounded in reality. 

 How Exemptions Work in Practice 
 CSA supports Exemptions for both SAP delivered checks and customer definable Custom Checks . Two types of Exemptions are supported. 
 Exempted Systems / Services 
 Removes specific systems or services from a check's scope, identified by their SID. Ideal for the grace period and accepted-risk scenarios above. 
 Every entry carries a validity period, a behaviour (Overrule or Ignore), and an automatically derived status. 
 Exempted Configuration Items 
 For checks where specific configuration item values needs to be treated as acceptable rather than non-compliant. 
 When a compliance rule does not fully specify all key field values, individual values can be explicitly exempted and treated as compliant for a defined scope and period. 

 Key behaviour’s: 
 Overrule (Compliant) -> the system shows as green in results, with a visible "exempted" indicator 
 Ignore -> the system is hidden entirely and excluded from compliance calculation 

 This is the right tool when selected items are explicitly known-good and should not count against compliance. 

 A Clear Lifecycle 
 Every exemption moves through a predictable lifecycle - Pending -> Active -> Expired , based on the validity period set by the Security Officer. Status transitions happen automatically, and multiple exemptions can exist on the same check if their periods don't overlap for the same scope. 

 Switching Between Views Instantly 
 The validation results view applies exemptions by default. A global Apply Exemptions toggle let’s any user switch instantly between: 
 With Exemptions (default): results reflect the overruled, process-compliant view 

 When a result is overruled as compliant, a dedicated column marks it as exempted, and the detail view shows a side-by-side comparison, so context is never lost. 

 Without Exemptions : results reflect the actual security posture 

 Summary 
 Exemptions in SAP Cloud ALM Configuration & Security Analysis give Security Officers the structured mechanism they need to maintain credible, useful compliance reports in the real world without sacrificing visibility into the actual security posture. Time-bound and role-governed, they bridge the gap between security policy and operational reality. 
 If you are a Security Officer managing compliance across a complex SAP landscape and have been working around the absence of a formal exemption mechanism, this feature is built for you. 
 Need help in creating a custom check yourself? Here you go Create Custom Checks . 
 For product questions or feedback on the Exemptions feature, reach out to us in the comments sections.

 Vijay

title: New Research Finds AI Is Moving Faster Than Organizations Can Adapt
author: Eric Annino
text:
Executives today face no shortage of pressure. 
 Run your business on an AI cloud ERP built for companies of any size 

 Learn how 

 Finance leaders are navigating capital constraints and economic uncertainty. Supply chain and operations leaders are balancing efficiency with resilience in an increasingly unpredictable environment. HR leaders are working to address critical skills gaps while preparing the workforce for new technologies. 

 Yet new research from Economist Enterprise sponsored by SAP—based on a survey of 2,015 C-suite executives at midsize organizations, those with revenues of $50 million to $1 billion, across the Americas, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific—found a common thread running through all three functions. For these organizations, AI adoption is consistently outpacing the people, processes, and capabilities needed to realize its full value. 

 Across finance, HR, and supply chain, the challenge is no longer whether to adopt AI. It’s how to ensure organizations are ready for it. 

 Across finance, HR, and supply chain, AI adoption is moving faster than the workforce, processes, and capabilities needed to support it. 

 Finance leaders see AI as an equalizer 

 For CFOs at midsize organizations, AI represents more than an efficiency opportunity. 

 Capital availability and financing costs rank among the most pressing concerns for 41% of finance leaders, a higher percentage than at larger organizations. Against that backdrop, AI is increasingly viewed as a way to help companies compete with organizations that have historically benefited from deeper resources. 

 Notably, reducing labor costs ranks last among CFOs’ AI objectives, cited by just 16% of respondents. Instead, finance leaders are focused on improving operational efficiency (41%), accelerating innovation (31%), and modernizing legacy systems (30%). 

 The challenge is execution. Sixty-six percent of CFOs say AI adoption is moving ahead of workforce transformation efforts. The findings suggest that finance leaders must play a broader role in transformation by connecting technology investments to the capabilities and skills required to generate value. 

 Sixty-six percent of CFOs say AI adoption is consistently running ahead of workforce transformation. 

 Read the full report: Advantage Under Pressure: How CFOs Are Navigating AI and Capital Trade-Offs 

 Supply chain and operations continue to gain influence 

 The research also highlights the growing strategic role of operations leaders. 

 Nearly half of C-suite executives rank supply chain, procurement, and operations among their organization’s three most influential functions, placing them on par with finance and behind only sales and technology. 

 That influence comes with growing responsibilities. Forty-three percent of operations leaders cite supply chain disruption as a top concern, while 38% point to operational resilience. Two in five identify balancing efficiency and resilience as their defining challenge, a figure that rises to 48% in manufacturing organizations. 

 AI presents significant potential, but results remain mixed. Only 47% of operations leaders at midsize companies report measurable value from AI investments, compared with 62% at organizations with revenues exceeding US$1 billion. 

 Just four percent say AI and workforce transformation are advancing as fully integrated initiatives, while 59% say AI adoption is moving ahead of workforce change. 

 The data suggests that organizations will create value not simply through AI investment, but through redesigning workflows, skills, and operating models around new technologies. 

 Only four percent of operations leaders say AI and workforce transformation are advancing as fully integrated initiatives. 

 Read the full report: Building for a World of What-Ifs: Navigating Resilience, Efficiency and Disruption 

 HR is taking on more responsibility than ever 

 No function is experiencing more rapid change than HR. 

 Nearly 74% of CHROs say their function is significantly more involved in workforce transformation than it was three years ago, the highest rate of change among C-suite functions. 

 The arrival of AI has intensified the challenge. More than half (54%) of CHROs identify workforce skills as the area least prepared for AI transformation. CHROs are also more than four times as likely as their executive peers to identify skills shortages as requiring immediate attention. 

 At the same time, many organizations are shifting budgets toward technology investments, creating additional pressure on HR teams to demonstrate their strategic value. 

 The opportunity for HR is significant. According to BCG , 70% of the effort required for AI transformation involves people and processes rather than technology itself. As organizations scale AI initiatives, workforce readiness may prove just as important as technological readiness. 

 Fifty-four percent of CHROs identify workforce skills as the area least prepared for AI transformation. 

 Read the full report: The Business of People: How CHROs Are Reshaping Tomorrow’s Workforce 

 The AI readiness gap is also an opportunity 

 Taken together, the three reports point to a common conclusion: organizations are moving quickly on AI, but often in fragmented ways. 

 Finance is deploying AI while workforce transformation struggles to keep pace. Operations is embedding AI into business processes while skills gaps persist. HR is working to prepare employees for a future arriving faster than many organizations expected. 

 For growing companies, this gap represents both a risk and an opportunity. Midsize organizations often have flatter structures and greater agility than larger enterprises, enabling them to align technology, people, and processes more quickly. 

 The research suggests that success will depend less on how much organizations invest in AI and more on how effectively they connect AI initiatives with workforce transformation and business process change. Organizations that integrate those efforts stand the best chance of turning AI investments into measurable business value. 

 The organizations generating the most value from AI aren’t necessarily investing more. They’re integrating technology, people, and processes more effectively.

title: What Manufacturers Can Learn from ifm’s Digital Manufacturing Journey
author: Anne Sailer
text:
For many manufacturers, years of growth have resulted in complex production environments. Site-specific applications, custom interfaces, and locally optimized processes often solve immediate business needs, but they can also make it more difficult to scale innovation, maintain systems, and drive consistency across a global production network. 

 Today, manufacturers are looking to simplify through standardized digital platforms that can support global operations, improve visibility, and provide a foundation for future innovation. 
 Boost automation and run autonomous manufacturing with SAP Digital Manufacturing 

 Learn more 

 When growth creates complexity 

 As a global manufacturer of sensor and automation technology with around 9,000 employees worldwide, ifm electronic GmbH operates multiple production sites across Germany and internationally. Over time, individual sites have developed their own integrations between operational technology (OT) systems and enterprise applications, creating a highly individualized manufacturing landscape. 

 While these local solutions addressed specific requirements, they also increased maintenance effort and complexity. As the company continued to grow, standardization became a strategic priority. 

 “We were looking for a standard to bring to all production sites and to make use of the solutions already available on the market,” Martin Haury, head of Global IT Business Services, ifm electronic GmbH, said. 

 Standardization as a strategic choice 

 When evaluating its future manufacturing landscape, ifm reviewed multiple manufacturing execution solutions and selected the SAP Digital Manufacturing solution. During the evaluation, the team discovered that many of the capabilities it had developed over the years—including production order execution, scheduling, and track-and-trace functionality—were already available as standard capabilities. According to Haury, the majority of more than 100 internally developed functionalities could be covered by the standard solution. 

 For ifm, the transformation was about more than just replacing custom applications. It was about establishing a standardized manufacturing foundation that could scale globally, increase transparency across operations, and support future innovation. The fact that so many internally developed capabilities were already available within SAP Digital Manufacturing helped accelerate that journey. 

 Less development, faster adoption 

 One of the most immediate benefits for ifm was the significant reduction in development effort. Rather than building and maintaining custom functionality, teams could make use of existing capabilities and configure them according to business requirements. 

 “Our OT colleagues were actually surprised that it’s just parameterizing and the solution is there,” Haury said. 

 Less development means less maintenance effort and a faster path from concept to deployment, helping ifm introduce standardized processes more efficiently across sites. 

 Building the future together 

 Throughout the implementation, cbs Corporate Business Solutions Unternehmensberatung GmbH supported ifm from both a manufacturing and a supply chain perspective. Beyond the technical implementation, the focus was on helping shape a future-ready manufacturing landscape that could scale across locations while remaining aligned with broader business processes. 

 Implementation partner 

 The implementation of SAP Digital Manufacturing was carried out in partnership with SAP partner cbs Corporate Business Solutions. The project focused on establishing standardized manufacturing processes and creating a scalable platform for future growth across ifm’s production operations. 

 Greater visibility across operations 

 Today, transparency is embedded far more deeply into ifm’s manufacturing operations. Production processes, manufacturing orders, and product availability are visible within a shared digital environment, enabling teams to work from the same information and respond more effectively to changing business requirements. 

 “Our implementation of SAP Digital Manufacturing is an important step in our digital transformation, setting the stage for a more connected, agile, and data-driven production environment,” Haury said. 

 As manufacturing networks become increasingly connected, access to consistent and reliable information is becoming essential for scaling operations and driving continuous improvement. 

 Looking ahead 

 Following a successful pilot deployment, ifm is preparing to expand the solution across its global production network. The company remains confident in both the approach and the long-term value it can deliver. 

 More important, the project highlights a broader lesson for manufacturers: the future of digital manufacturing is not about building every capability from scratch. It is about using proven standards, simplifying complexity, and creating a foundation that enables innovation to scale. 

 For manufacturers evaluating their own transformation journey, standardization is no longer just an IT objective. It is a business strategy for increasing transparency, reducing complexity, and preparing operations for future growth. “We were looking for a standard to bring to all production sites and to make use of integrated solution with seamless data-flow and clear innovation track, like AI,” Haury said.
